nodes.name: Half-Laplacian via the Lévy-Khintchine formula
nodes.statement: Let us set the one-dimensional half-Laplacian operator $L$ defined on functions $w\in L^\infty (\hbox{\bf R})\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta<1$ by the L\'evy-Khintchine formula $$Lw(x)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\hbox{\bf R}}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x+z)-w(x)-zw'(x) 1_{\left\{|z|\le 1\right\}}\right).$$
nodes.statement_short: The half-Laplacian $L$ on $L^\infty\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}$ functions, defined by the Lévy-Khintchine integral with kernel $dz/z^2$.

nodes.name: Layer solution of the Peierls-Nabarro model
nodes.statement: Given a suitable $1$-periodic potential $W$ which satisfies in particular $W'(k)=0$ for $k\in\hbox{\bf Z}$ ($W$ will be precised later in assumption \textbf{(A)}), it is known (see Section \ref{subsection-layer}) that there exists a unique solution $\phi$ of \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\phi -W'(\phi)=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R},\\ \displaystyle{\phi'>0 \quad \mbox{and}\quad \phi(-\infty)=0,\quad \phi(0)=\frac 1 2,\quad \phi(+\infty)=1.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: For a periodic potential $W$ vanishing derivative on integers, $\phi$ is the unique increasing layer solution of $L\phi=W'(\phi)$ from 0 to 1.

nodes.name: Peierls-Nabarro layer equation
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\phi -W'(\phi)=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R},\\ \displaystyle{\phi'>0 \quad \mbox{and}\quad \phi(-\infty)=0,\quad \phi(0)=\frac 1 2,\quad \phi(+\infty)=1.} \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq::0

nodes.name: Peierls-Nabarro model; stacking fault energy
nodes.statement: Model \eqref{eq::0} is known as the Peierls-Nabarro model for dislocations in crystals where $W$ is called the stacking fault energy.

nodes.name: Evolution problem for the Peierls-Nabarro model; exterior stress
nodes.statement: We now consider a scalar function $v$ solution of the following evolution problem associated to the Peierls-Nabarro model: \begin{equation} v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} where $\sigma^\varepsilon$ is the exterior stress acting in the material.

nodes.name: Reaction-diffusion equation with half-Laplacian
nodes.statement: v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}
nodes.label: eq::901

nodes.name: Scaling of the exterior stress
nodes.statement: We assume that this exterior stress is given for $\varepsilon>0$ small, by $$\sigma^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon\sigma\left(\frac{t}{\varepsilon^2},\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right)$$ where $\sigma$ is a given suitable function.

nodes.name: Rescaled solution $v^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: Then we can consider the following rescaling $$v^\varepsilon(t,x)=v\left(\frac{t}{\varepsilon^2},\frac{x}{\varepsilon}\right).$$

nodes.name: Rescaled evolution problem
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{Lv^\varepsilon-\frac{1}{\varepsilon}W'(v^\varepsilon) + \sigma(t,x)\right\} \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}}\\ \\ v^\varepsilon(0,x)=v^\varepsilon_0(x) \quad \mbox{for}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}. \end{array}\right.
nodes.statement_short: Rescaled reaction-diffusion equation $v^\varepsilon_t=\varepsilon^{-1}(Lv^\varepsilon-\varepsilon^{-1}W'(v^\varepsilon)+\sigma)$ with initial datum.
nodes.label: eq::1

nodes.name: ODE system of particles with $1/x$ interactions
nodes.statement: When $v^\varepsilon$ has $N$ transition layers as $\varepsilon$ goes to zero, we will see that we can associate a particle to each transition layer such that the dynamics of $v^\varepsilon$ is driven by the following ODE system for particles $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$: \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\frac{dx_i}{dt}}= \gamma \left(-\sigma(t,x_i) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{x_i-x_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty),\\ x_i(0)=x_i^0, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N \end{equation} where \begin{equation} \gamma = \left(\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2\right)^{-1}. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Particles $x_i$ move with velocity $\gamma(-\sigma(t,x_i)+\frac1\pi\sum_{j\ne i}\frac{1}{x_i-x_j})$, $\gamma=(\int(\phi')^2)^{-1}$.

nodes.name: Particle ODE system
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\frac{dx_i}{dt}}= \gamma \left(-\sigma(t,x_i) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{x_i-x_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty),\\ x_i(0)=x_i^0, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N
nodes.label: eq::2

nodes.name: Mobility constant $\gamma$
nodes.statement: \gamma = \left(\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2\right)^{-1}.
nodes.label: eq::2'

nodes.name: Assumption (A i): periodic potential
nodes.statement: To state precisely our main result, we make the following assumptions:\\ \noindent {\bf(A)}\\ \noindent {\bf i) Assumption on the potential}\\ $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} W\in C^{2,\beta}(\hbox{\bf R}) \quad \mbox{for some}\quad 0<\beta<1,\\ \\ W(v+1)=W(v) \quad \mbox{for any}\quad v\in\hbox{\bf R},\\ \\ W=0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad\hbox{\bf Z},\\ \\ W>0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad\hbox{\bf R}\backslash \hbox{\bf Z},\\ \\ W''(0)>0. \end{array}\right.$$
nodes.statement_short: $W$ is $C^{2,\beta}$, 1-periodic, vanishes exactly on $\mathbf Z$ and has $W''(0)>0$.

nodes.name: Assumption (A ii): exterior stress
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf ii) Assumption on the exterior stress} $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \sigma \in BUC\left([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R}\right) \quad \mbox{and for some}\quad 0<\beta<1 \quad \mbox{and}\quad K>0, \quad \mbox{we have}\\ \\ |\sigma_x|_{L^\infty ([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R})}\le K, \quad |\sigma_t|_{L^\infty ([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R})}\le K,\\ \\ |\sigma_x(t,x+h)-\sigma_x(t,x)|\le K |h|^\beta \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x,h\in\hbox{\bf R},\quad t\in [0,+\infty ). \end{array}\right.$$ We recall that BUC is the space of bounded uniformly continuous functions.
nodes.statement_short: $\sigma$ is bounded uniformly continuous with bounded $\sigma_x,\sigma_t$ and $\sigma_x$ $\beta$-Hölder in space.

nodes.name: Assumption (A iii): well-prepared initial condition
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf iii) Assumption on the initial condition} \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} \mbox{For}\quad x_1^0< x_2^0< ...<x^0_N, \quad \mbox{we set}\\ \\ \displaystyle{v_0^\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(0,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0.} \end{array}\right. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Initial datum is a sum of $N$ rescaled layers at ordered points $x_i^0$ plus the correction $\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(0,x)$, $\alpha=W''(0)$.

nodes.name: Initial condition $v_0^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} \mbox{For}\quad x_1^0< x_2^0< ...<x^0_N, \quad \mbox{we set}\\ \\ \displaystyle{v_0^\varepsilon(x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(0,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0.} \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq::900

nodes.name: Convergence to the ODE system
nodes.statement: {\bf (Convergence to the ODE system)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2}). Let $$v^0(t,x)= \sum_{i=1}^N H(x-x_i(t))$$ where $H(x)=1_{[0,+\infty)}(x)$ is the Heaviside function. Then for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a unique viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1}). Moreover as $\varepsilon \to 0$, $v^\varepsilon$ converges to $v^0$ in the following sense: \begin{equation} \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\geq (v^0)_* (t,x) \end{equation} for $(t,x)\in [0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Under (A), the viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ converges as $\varepsilon\to0$ to a sum of Heaviside jumps at particles solving the ODE system.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2})
for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists a unique viscosity solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1})

as $\varepsilon \to 0$, $v^\varepsilon$ converges to $v^0$ in the following sense: \begin{equation} \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x) \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\geq (v^0)_* (t,x) \end{equation} for $(t,x)\in [0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R}$
nodes.label: th::1

nodes.name: Upper limit bound
nodes.statement: \limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\leq (v^0)^* (t,x)
nodes.label: eq::c+

nodes.name: Lower limit bound
nodes.statement: \liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x),\ \epsilon\to 0} v^{\epsilon}(t',x')\geq (v^0)_* (t,x)
nodes.label: eq::c-

nodes.name: Semi-continuous envelopes
nodes.statement: We recall here that the semi-continuous envelopes of a given any function $u$ are defined as follows $$u^*(t,x)=\limsup_{(t',x')\to(t,x)} u(t',x')\quad\quad\mbox{and}\quad\quad u_*(t,x)=\liminf_{(t',x')\to(t,x)} u(t',x').$$

nodes.name: Ansatz for the solution
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{th::1} is done by constructing suitable sub and supersolutions essentially based on the following ansatz of the solution: \begin{equation} \tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(t,x)+\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)-\varepsilon \dot{x}_i(t)\ \psi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\} \end{equation} where $\psi$ is a suitable corrector.
nodes.statement_short: Ansatz: $\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma$ plus sum of layers $\phi$ at $x_i(t)$, each corrected by $-\varepsilon\dot x_i\psi$.

nodes.name: Ansatz formula
nodes.statement: \tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\frac{\varepsilon}{\alpha}\sigma(t,x)+\sum_{i=1}^N \left\{ \phi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)-\varepsilon \dot{x}_i(t)\ \psi\left(\frac{x-x_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\}
nodes.label: eq::an

nodes.name: Alberti-Bouchitté-Seppecher Gamma-convergence theorem
nodes.statement: They have shown in \cite{Alberti-Bouchitte-Seppecher:singular-perturbations} that if we consider the energy functional for $\Omega\subset\mathbb R^n$ and a double well potential $W$ given by $$E_\epsilon[u]=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u}^2+\frac{1}{\epsilon}\int_{\partial\Omega}W(u)$$ then, in particular, the rescalings $E_\epsilon[u]/\abs{\log\epsilon}$ Gamma-converge when $\epsilon\to 0$ to $\frac{2}{\pi}\mathcal H^0(S_{u_0})$ if $n=2$ (thus $\partial\Omega$ is one dimensional) and the minimizers $u_\epsilon$ converge to $u_0$, where $u_0=0,1$ on $\partial\Omega$, $\Delta u_0=0$ in $\Omega$, and the singular set is $$S_{u_0}=\left\{ z\in\partial\Omega \mbox{ : }u_0 \mbox{ jumps at }z \right\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Boundary double-well energies rescaled by $|\log\epsilon|$ Gamma-converge to $\frac2\pi$ times the number of jumps; minimizers converge.

nodes.name: Convergence for fractional Laplacians $(-\Delta)^\alpha$
nodes.statement: We expect (even if we have no proof) Theorem \ref{th::1} to be true for any power of the Laplacian $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, once the layer solutions of \eqref{eq::0} are found.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 1.1 should hold for any power $(-\Delta)^\alpha$, $\alpha\in(0,1)$, once layer solutions exist.

nodes.name: Evolution problem with $\varepsilon=1$
nodes.statement: \left\{ \begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{v_t=Lv-W'(v) + \sigma(t,x) \quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}}\\ v(0,x)=v_0(x) \quad \mbox{for}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}. \end{array}\right.
nodes.label: eq::1ter

nodes.name: Viscosity sub and supersolutions
nodes.statement: {\bf (Viscosity sub and supersolutions)}\\ An upper (respectively lower) semicontinuous function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})$ is said to be a subsolution (resp. a supersolution) of (\ref{eq::1ter}) if and only if $$v(0,\cdot)\le v_0^* \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R}$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad v(0,\cdot)\ge v_0^* \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R}\right)$$ and for any $C^2$ test function $\varphi$ satisfying $$v= \varphi \quad \mbox{at the point}\quad (t_0,x_0)\in (0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$$ and $$ v\le \varphi \quad \mbox{on a neighborhood of}\quad \left\{t_0\right\}\times \hbox{\bf R}$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad v\ge \varphi \quad \mbox{on a neighborhood of}\quad \left\{t_0\right\}\times \hbox{\bf R}\right)$$ then we have $$\varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \le L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0)$$ $$\left(\mbox{resp.}\quad \varphi_t(t_0,x_0) \ge L^1[\varphi(t_0,\cdot),v(t_0,\cdot)](x_0) -W'(\varphi(t_0,x_0)) + \sigma(t_0,x_0) \right)$$ where for any functions $\Phi(x), w(x)$ we set $$L^1[\Phi,w](x_0)=\frac{1}{\pi} \int_{[-1,1]}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(\Phi(x_0+z)-\Phi(x_0)-z\Phi'(x_0) \right) + \frac{1}{\pi} \int_{\hbox{\bf R}\backslash [-1,1]}\frac{dz}{z^2}\left(w(x_0+z)-w(x_0)\right).$$ A function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})$ is said to be a viscosity solution of (\ref{eq::1ter}), if and only if $v^*$ is a subsolution and $v_*$ is a supersolution.\\ Finally, a function $v\in L^\infty_{loc}([0,+\infty )\times \hbox{\bf R})$ is said to be a viscosity solution on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$, if and only if its is a viscosity solution on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$ for any $T>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Viscosity sub/supersolutions of the nonlocal equation via $C^2$ test functions touching from above/below, with the split operator $L^1[\varphi,v]$.
nodes.label: defi::1

nodes.name: Classical solutions are viscosity solutions
nodes.statement: {\bf (Classical solutions are viscosity solutions)}\\ From this definition, we can easily check that every function $v\in L^\infty([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})\cap C^{1,\beta}_{loc}([0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta<1$, is indeed a viscosity solution if and only if it is a classical solution of (\ref{eq::1ter}). This is mainly due to the fact that $v_t$ and $Lv(t,\cdot)$ are then defined pointwise.

nodes.name: Perron's method
nodes.statement: {\bf (Perron's method)}\\ Assume that there exists a supersolution $\underline{v}$ and a subsolution $\overline{v}$ of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$ Then there exists a viscosity solution $v$ of (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le v\le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
assumptions: there exists a supersolution $\underline{v}$ and a subsolution $\overline{v}$ of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
conclusions: there exists a viscosity solution $v$ of (\ref{eq::1ter}) satisfying $$\underline{v} \le v\le \overline{v} \quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
nodes.label: pro::v1

nodes.name: Comparison principle
nodes.statement: {\bf (Comparison principle)}\\ Assume that $\underline{v}$ is a subsolution (resp. $\overline{v}$ is a supersolution) of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) on $[0,T)$ such that $$\underline{v}(0,x)\le \overline{v}(0,x)\quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in \hbox{\bf R}.$$ Then $$\underline{v}\le \overline{v}\quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
assumptions: $\underline{v}$ is a subsolution (resp. $\overline{v}$ is a supersolution) of equation (\ref{eq::1ter}) on $[0,T)$ such that $$\underline{v}(0,x)\le \overline{v}(0,x)\quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in \hbox{\bf R}.$$
conclusions: $$\underline{v}\le \overline{v}\quad \mbox{on}\quad [0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}.$$
nodes.label: pro:4

nodes.name: Uniqueness and continuity from the comparison principle
nodes.statement: In particular, when the initial data $v_0$ is continuous, the comparison principle implies the uniqueness and the continuity of the solution.
conclusions: the uniqueness and the continuity of the solution

nodes.name: First try for the ansatz (formal)
nodes.statement: Namely, we are looking for an ansatz for the solutions of \begin{equation} \displaystyle{-\varepsilon v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(v^\varepsilon) -\varepsilon Lv^\varepsilon - \varepsilon \sigma \right\}\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}.} \end{equation} Assume to simplify that $\sigma$ is a constant here, and that there is only one transition layer.\\ \noindent {\bf First try for the ansatz}\\ As a first try, in the case where $\tilde{\sigma}$ is constant, we could consider the Ansatz $$\tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi\left(\frac{x-x_1(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)$$ where $\phi$ is the transition layer solution of \begin{equation} L\phi-W'(\phi)=0. \end{equation} When we plug this expression in (\ref{eq::13}), we get $$\begin{array}{lcl} \dot{x}_1\phi' &\simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi) - L\phi -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi) - W'(\phi) -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq & \displaystyle{W''(\phi) \tilde{\sigma} -\sigma + O(\varepsilon)}\\ \end{array}$$ where we have used (\ref{eq::14}) for the second line, and a Taylor expansion to get the third line. From this computation, we learn two things. First for $\phi \simeq 0$ we have to choose \begin{equation} W''(0) \tilde{\sigma} =\sigma. \end{equation} The second information, is that it is impossible to satisfy the equation with this ansatz, and we need to introduce a corrector.
nodes.statement_short: Plugging a pure layer ansatz into the equation forces $W''(0)\tilde\sigma=\sigma$ and shows a corrector is needed.

nodes.name: Equation for the formal ansatz
nodes.statement: \displaystyle{-\varepsilon v^\varepsilon_t=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(v^\varepsilon) -\varepsilon Lv^\varepsilon - \varepsilon \sigma \right\}\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}.}
nodes.label: eq::13

nodes.name: Layer equation $L\phi=W'(\phi)$
nodes.statement: L\phi-W'(\phi)=0.
nodes.label: eq::14

nodes.name: Choice of $\tilde\sigma$
nodes.statement: W''(0) \tilde{\sigma} =\sigma.
nodes.label: eq::15

nodes.name: Second try for the ansatz (formal)
nodes.statement: \noindent {\bf Second try for the ansatz}\\ Let us take $$\tilde{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi\left(\frac{x-x_1(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) -\varepsilon c \psi\left(\frac{x-x_1(t)}{\varepsilon}\right)$$ for $\tilde{\sigma}$ satisfying (\ref{eq::15}) and for some constant $c$ to fix later. When we plug this expression in (\ref{eq::13}), we get $$\begin{array}{lcl} \dot{x}_1\phi' +h.o.t. &\simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi -\varepsilon c\psi) - L\phi +c\varepsilon L\psi -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq &\displaystyle{\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\left\{W'(\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma} + \phi -\varepsilon c\psi) - W'(\phi) +c\varepsilon L\psi -\varepsilon \sigma\right\}}\\ \\ & \simeq & W''(\phi) (\tilde{\sigma}-c\psi) -\sigma +c L\psi + h.o.t. \end{array}$$ where we have used a Taylor expansion to get the last line. Finally using (\ref{eq::15}), we see that $\psi$ has to solve \begin{equation} L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi = \frac{\dot{x}_1}{c} \phi' - \frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c}(W''(\phi)-W''(0)). \end{equation} We see that it is convenient to choose (in order to get later $\psi$ independent on $\dot{x}_1$) $$\dot{x}_1=c.$$ Moreover, multiplying (\ref{eq::16}) by $\phi'$ we get formally by integration: $$\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \phi'\left(L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi\right)} & = &\displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} (\phi')^2 -\frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c} \left( \int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \frac{d}{dx}(W'(\phi(x)) - W''(0)\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \phi'\right)}\\ \\ & = & \displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} (\phi')^2 +\frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c} W''(0).} \end{array}$$ On the other hand using the fact that $L$ is self-adjoint, we get formally $$\begin{array}{lcl} \displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \phi'\left(L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi\right)} &= &\displaystyle{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}} \psi\left(L\phi' - W''(\phi)\phi'\right)}\\ \\ &=& 0. \end{array}$$ where the last equality comes from the fact that $\phi$ solves (\ref{eq::14}) so then $\phi'$ solves $$L\phi'-W''(\phi)\phi'=0.$$ Therefore, we get $$c=-\gamma \sigma \quad \mbox{with}\quad \gamma= \left(\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2\right)^{-1}$$ and $\psi$ solves $$L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi = \phi' +\eta (W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \eta= \frac{1}{\gamma W''(0)}.$$
nodes.statement_short: With a corrector term, solvability (Fredholm alternative against $\phi'$) gives velocity $c=-\gamma\sigma$ and the corrector equation for $\psi$.

nodes.name: Formal corrector equation
nodes.statement: L\psi - W''(\phi)\psi = \frac{\dot{x}_1}{c} \phi' - \frac{\tilde{\sigma}}{c}(W''(\phi)-W''(0)).
nodes.label: eq::16

nodes.name: Existence and properties of the layer solution
nodes.statement: {\bf (Existence and properties of the layer solution)}\\ Under assumption Ai), there exists a unique solution $\phi$ of (\ref{eq::0bis}). Moreover $\phi \in C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta <1$, and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \begin{equation} 0<\phi'(x)\le \frac{C}{1+x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \left|\phi(x)-H(x)+\frac{1}{\alpha \pi x}\right| \quad \le \quad \frac{C}{x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad |x|\ge 1 \end{equation} where $H$ is the Heaviside function and $\alpha=W''(0)$.
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.statement_short: Under (A i) the layer solution $\phi$ exists uniquely, is $C^{1,\beta}$, with $\phi'\lesssim 1/(1+x^2)$ and $\phi=H-\frac{1}{\alpha\pi x}+O(x^{-2})$.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $\phi$ of (\ref{eq::0bis})

$\phi \in C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta <1$, and there exists a constant $C>0$ such that \begin{equation} 0<\phi'(x)\le \frac{C}{1+x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} and \begin{equation} \left|\phi(x)-H(x)+\frac{1}{\alpha \pi x}\right| \quad \le \quad \frac{C}{x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad |x|\ge 1 \end{equation} where $H$ is the Heaviside function and $\alpha=W''(0)$
nodes.label: th::5

nodes.name: Decay of $\phi'$
nodes.statement: 0<\phi'(x)\le \frac{C}{1+x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.label: eq::5

nodes.name: Asymptotics of the layer solution
nodes.statement: \left|\phi(x)-H(x)+\frac{1}{\alpha \pi x}\right| \quad \le \quad \frac{C}{x^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad |x|\ge 1
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.label: eq::6

nodes.name: Corrector $\psi$
nodes.statement: We are also looking for a corrector $\psi$, solution of the following equation \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\psi -W''(\phi)\psi=\phi'+ \eta (W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R},\\ \psi(-\infty)=0 = \psi(+\infty) \end{array}\right. \end{equation} with \begin{equation} \eta = \frac{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2}{W''(0)}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.statement_short: The corrector $\psi$ solves the linearized equation $L\psi-W''(\phi)\psi=\phi'+\eta(W''(\phi)-W''(0))$, vanishing at $\pm\infty$.

nodes.name: Corrector equation
nodes.statement: \left\{\begin{array}{l} L\psi -W''(\phi)\psi=\phi'+ \eta (W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{on}\quad \hbox{\bf R},\\ \psi(-\infty)=0 = \psi(+\infty) \end{array}\right.
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.label: eq::7

nodes.name: Constant $\eta$
nodes.statement: \eta = \frac{\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}(\phi')^2}{W''(0)}.
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.label: eq::7'

nodes.name: Existence and properties of the corrector
nodes.statement: {\bf (Existence and properties of the corrector)}\\ Under assumption Ai), there exists a unique solution $\psi \in H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ of (\ref{eq::7}). Moreover $\psi \in C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})\cap L^\infty (\hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta< 1$ and $$|\psi'|_{L^\infty(\hbox{\bf R})} < +\infty. $$
nodes.section: 3.2 The layer solution and the corrector
nodes.statement_short: Under (A i) the corrector equation has a unique $H^{1/2}$ solution, which is $C^{1,\beta}_{loc}$, bounded, with bounded derivative.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $\psi \in H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$ of (\ref{eq::7})
$\psi \in C^{1,\beta}_{loc}(\hbox{\bf R})\cap L^\infty (\hbox{\bf R})$ for some $0<\beta< 1$ and $$|\psi'|_{L^\infty(\hbox{\bf R})} < +\infty. $$
nodes.label: th::6

nodes.name: Lower bound on the distance between particles
nodes.statement: {\bf (Lower bound on the distance between particles, \cite{Forcadel-Imbert-Monneau:homogeneization})}\\ Let $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ be the solution of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,T]$ and let $$d(t):=\min\{\abs{x_i(t)-x_j(t)},i\neq j\}$$ be the minimal distance between particles. Then under assumptions Ai) and Aii), we have for all $t\in [0,T]$ $$d(t)\ge d(0) e^{-Ct} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C=\gamma K$$ where $K$ is the space Lipschitz constant of $\sigma$.
conclusions: for all $t\in [0,T]$ $$d(t)\ge d(0) e^{-Ct} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C=\gamma K$$ where $K$ is the space Lipschitz constant of $\sigma$.
nodes.label: lem::1

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 3.4 (long time existence)
nodes.statement: This lemma prevents the crossing of particles in finite time. As a consequence, we easily get the following long time existence result:
nodes.statement_short: No crossing of particles by the distance lower bound, so the local solution extends to all times.

nodes.name: Long time existence of a solution to the ODE system
nodes.statement: {\bf (Long time existence of a solution to the ODE system)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,+\infty)$.
conclusions: there exists a unique solution $(x_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ of (\ref{eq::2bis}) on $[0,+\infty)$.
nodes.label: cor::1

nodes.name: Perturbed particle trajectories $\overline{x}_i$
nodes.statement: We define $(\overline{x}_i(t))_{i=1,...,N}$ as the solution of $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \displaystyle{\frac{d\overline{x}_i}{dt}= \gamma \left(-\delta-\sigma(\overline{x}_i,t) + \frac{1}{\pi}\sum_{j\not= i} \frac{1}{\overline{x}_i-\overline{x}_j}\right),\quad \mbox{on}\quad (0,+\infty)},\\ \overline{x}_i(0)=x_i^0-\delta, \end{array}\right| \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N$$ with $\gamma$ given in (\ref{eq::2'}).
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Trajectories of the ODE system with extra stress $\delta$ and initial points shifted by $-\delta$.

nodes.name: Supersolution ansatz $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: We also define $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x)=\varepsilon \tilde{\sigma}(t,x) + \sum_{i=1}^N \left\{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) -\varepsilon\overline{c}_i(t)\psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(t)}{\varepsilon}\right) \right\}$$ where $$\left\{\begin{array}{l} \overline{c}_i(t) = \dot{\overline{x}}_i(t)\\ \\ \displaystyle{\tilde{\sigma}=\frac{\delta+\sigma}{\alpha} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \alpha=W''(0)>0} \end{array}\right.$$ and $\phi$ is given in Theorem \ref{th::5} and $\psi$ in Theorem \ref{th::6}.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Supersolution candidate built from layers at $\overline x_i$ with correctors weighted by velocities $\overline c_i=\dot{\overline x}_i$.

nodes.name: Supersolution at the initial time
nodes.statement: {\bf (Supersolution at the initial time)}\\ Under assumption (A), there exists $\delta_0>0$ such that for all $0<\delta\le \delta_0$, we have \begin{equation} \overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R} \end{equation} for $\varepsilon >0$ small enough.
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
conclusions: \overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}
nodes.label: pro::2

nodes.name: Initial ordering $\overline v^\varepsilon\ge v_0^\varepsilon$
nodes.statement: \overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.label: eq::8

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 4.1
nodes.statement: \\ First we choose $\delta>0$ small enough such that $$x^0_i<\overline{x}_{i+1}(0)< x_{i+1}^0 \quad \mbox{for}\quad i=1,...,N-1.$$ Let $A>0$ be large enough such that \begin{equation} \frac{\delta}{\alpha} \ge \left(\sum_{i=1}^N |\overline{c}_i(0)|\right)\ \sup_{\hbox{\bf R}\backslash [-A,A]} |\psi|. \end{equation} \noindent {\bf Case 1: $|x-\overline{x}_i(0)|\ge \varepsilon A$ for each $i=1,...,N$}\\ Using the fact that $\phi$ is increasing, we deduce that $\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right)}$ and then using (\ref{eq::10}), we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$ \noindent {\bf Case 2: $|x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)| < \varepsilon A$ for some index $i_0\in \left\{1,...,N\right\}$}\\ Then $$\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)\ge \phi(-A)>0$$ while $$\begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right)} & = \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)-\delta}{\varepsilon}\right)}\\ \\ & \displaystyle{\le \phi\left(A-\frac{\delta}{\varepsilon}\right) = O\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right) \quad \mbox{as}\quad \varepsilon \to 0.} \end{array}$$ Therefore for $\varepsilon$ small enough, we have $$\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right) +\sum_{i=1}^N \varepsilon \overline{c}_i(0) \psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)}.$$ Using again the monotonicity of $\phi$, we conclude in case 2 that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$ Finally case 1 and 2 prove that (\ref{eq::8}) holds for any $x\in\hbox{\bf R}$. This ends the proof of the Proposition. \qed
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement_short: Case analysis on the distance of $x$ to the shifted particles, using monotonicity of $\phi$ and smallness of the corrector away from layers.

nodes.name: Choice of $A$
nodes.statement: \frac{\delta}{\alpha} \ge \left(\sum_{i=1}^N |\overline{c}_i(0)|\right)\ \sup_{\hbox{\bf R}\backslash [-A,A]} |\psi|.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.1
nodes.statement: \\ \noindent {\bf Step 1: existence and uniqueness of the solution}\\ First remark that for $\varepsilon$ small enough the initial condition satisfies $$-1\le v^\varepsilon_0 \le N+1$$ and the functions $$\underline{u}(t,x)=-1-K^\varepsilon t \quad \mbox{and}\quad \overline{u}(t,x)=N+1+K^\varepsilon t$$ with $$K^\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}|\sigma|_{L^\infty([0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R})} +\varepsilon^{-2} |W'|_{L^\infty(\hbox{\bf R})}$$ are respectively sub and supersolutions of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. From the Perron's method, it follows the existence of a solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$ which is moreover unique thanks to the comparison principle (Proposition \ref{pro:4}).\\ \noindent {\bf Step 2: sub and supersolutions as $\varepsilon \to 0$}\\ Now, given any fixed $T>0$, and thanks to Propositions \ref{pro::2} and \ref{pro::3}, we can find some $\delta>0$ small enough such that $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ is a supersolution of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$.\\ Similarly we can build a subsolution $\underline{v}^\varepsilon$ (defined simply as $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ but with $\delta <0$). At the initial time we have $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ and then from the comparison principle, we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad t\in [0,T),\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}.$$ Now for fixed $T>0$, we get the result (namely (\ref{eq::c+}) and (\ref{eq::c-})) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$, passing to the limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Finally, because $T>0$ was arbitrary, we recover the result for all time on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. This ends the proof of the Theorem.\qed

nodes.name: Fourier transform and the space $H^{\frac12}(\mathbf R)$
nodes.statement: We recall our definition of the Fourier transform for $w \in {\mathcal S}(\hbox{\bf R})$ (where ${\mathcal S}(\hbox{\bf R})$ is the Schwartz space): $$\widehat{w}(\xi)=\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}w(x) \ e^{-i\xi x}dx \quad \mbox{for all}\quad \xi\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ and recall the definition of the following Hilbert space $$H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})=\left\{w\in L^2(\hbox{\bf R}),\quad \int_{\hbox{\bf R}}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)|\widehat{w}(\xi)|^2 < +\infty \right\}$$ with the scalar product $$(v,w)_{H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})}=\int_{\hbox{\bf R}}d\xi\ (1+|\xi|)\widehat{v}^*(\xi) \widehat{w}(\xi)$$ where $\widehat{v}^*$ denotes here the complex conjugate of $\widehat{v}$.

nodes.name: The space $H^{-\frac12}(\mathbf R)$

nodes.statement: We say that $u$ is a \emph{layer solution} of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} if it satisfies \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer}, $u_x>0$ on $\partial\Omega$ and $$\lim_{x \to -\infty} u(x,0)=0,\quad \lim_{x\to +\infty} u(x,0)=1.$$

nodes.name: Known existence and properties of the layer solution
nodes.statement: {\bf (Known existence and properties of the layer solution)}\\ Let $f$ be any $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}$ function with $0 < \beta < 1$ and such that $W'= -f$. Then there exists a layer solution $u_W\in \mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$ of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} if and only if $$W'(0)=W'(1)=0\quad\mbox{and}\quad W> W(0)=W(1)\quad\mbox{in } (0,1).$$ Moreover, \begin{enumerate} \item If $W''(0), W''(1)>0$, then a layer solution of \eqref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer} is unique up to translations in the $x$ variable, and it satisfies \begin{equation}(u_W)_x>0\quad\mbox{in }\overline{\Omega}.\end{equation} \item We have the estimate \begin{equation}\abs{\nabla u_W(x,y)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{(x,y)}}, \quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, y\geq 0.\end{equation} \item Set $\phi(x):=u_W(x,0)$. We have the bounds \begin{equation} \abs{\phi(x)-H(x)}\leq \frac{C}{1+\abs{x}} \quad\mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, \end{equation} \begin{equation} \frac{C_1}{1+\abs{x}^2} \leq \phi'(x)\leq \frac{C_2}{1+\abs{x}^2},\quad \mbox{for all }x\in\mathbb R, \end{equation} for some positive constants $C,C_1,C_2$. \item A layer solution is always a stable solution. This means that \begin{equation}\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla v}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)v^2\geq 0\end{equation} for every function $v\in\mathcal C^1(\overline{\Omega})$ with compact support in $\overline{\Omega}$.\\ \end{enumerate}

nodes.statement: This is a small variation of the classical proof for the Laplacian, that can be found in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, Theorem 8.1. Note that $(Tu)^-= T(u^-)$ a.e. in $\mathbb R$. Set $$\Omega^-:=supp (u^-)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Theta:=supp((Tu)^-)\subset \mathbb R.$$ We know that $\Omega^-$ is contained in $\mathbb R^2_+\backslash B_R^+$ and $\Theta\subset \mathbb R\backslash(-R,R)$. Use $u^-\in H$ as an admissible test function in \eqref{weak-super-solution}; then $$0\leq -\int_{\Omega^-} \abs{\nabla u}^2-\int_{\Theta}d(x)u^2.$$ The proof is easily completed.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.16
nodes.statement: We use Proposition \ref{prop-moser-iteration} with some modifications in order to account for the extra right hand side term involving $g$. By hypothesis, $w$ is a weak solution satisfying for all $v\in H$, $$B(u,v)=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gv, \quad\mbox{for }u=P*_x w.$$ Similarly as before (using if necessary a truncated version), we use the test function $v=\abs{u}^{\sigma-1} u$, $u_1=|u|^{\gamma-1}u$ and $w_1 = Tu_1$. We use H\"older inequality with exponents $2\gamma$, $\frac{2\gamma}{2\gamma-1}$, which gives $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} gv}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{g}^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\right)^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}},$$ we get \begin{equation*}\begin{split} \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 &\le C_1(\gamma) \int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2} +\tilde{C}_1(\gamma)\left(\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\right)^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}}\quad \mbox{with}\quad \tilde{C}_1(\gamma)= \frac{\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}\cdot \left(\int_{\partial \Omega} |g|^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}. \end{split}\end{equation*} Assuming (\ref{eq::904}) with $2\gamma\ge p_0$, we get $$\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 \le \bar{C}_1(\gamma) \max\left\{1,\int_{\partial \Omega} w_1^2\right\} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \bar{C}_1(\gamma) = C_1(\gamma) + \frac{c\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}$$ The rest of the argument follows similarly, with $\bar{C}_2(\gamma)=\max\left\{1,C_p(1+2\pi \bar{C}_1(\gamma))\right\}$, $\bar\Psi(q)=\max \left\{1,\left(\int_{\partial\Omega}|w|^q\right)^{\frac1q}\right\}$, and $\bar \Psi(2p\gamma)\le (\bar C_2(\gamma))^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\bar \Psi(2\gamma)$, starting the iteration at $2\gamma=p_0$.\qed\\

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement:
Let $W$ be a potential satisfying hypothesis \emph{Ai)}. Theorem ef{thm-layer-solutions} shows existence, regularity, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of a layer solution $0<u_W<1$ satisfying $u_W(0,0)=1/2$, $u\in\mathcal C^{2, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline{\Omega})$, for the problem  egin{equation} \left\{ egin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\  rac{\partial u}{\partial 
u} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}ight.\end{equation} We denote its trace value by $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$. The aim of the next paragraphs is to show the more precise estimate \eqref{eq::6} for the asymptotic behavior near infinity.\ Set $a=1/\alpha$, where $\alpha=W''(0)$ as defined in (ef{eq::900}), and choose the model layer solution $u^a$ as given in \eqref{model-layer}. We know explicitly because of \eqref{asymptotic-layer} that $\phi^a:=u^a(\cdot,0)$ has the right asymptotic behavior \eqref{eq::6}. We would like to compare $u_W$ to $u^a$, in order to obtain the analogous estimate for $u_W$. Therefore, we set $v:=u_W-u^a$. Then $v$ satisfies  egin{equation*}\left\{ egin{split} &\Delta v= \;0 \quad &\mbox{in } \Omega,\ & rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u}= -W'(\phi)+V'_a(\phi^a)\quad &\mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}ight. \end{equation*} Now we estimate $$-W'(\phi)+W'(\phi^a)=-W''(0)[\phi-\phi^a]+O\left(  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}ight),$$ thanks to the growth estimate \eqref{growth-not-sharp}. And also, $$-W'(\phi^a)+V'_a(\phi^a)=[-W''(0)+V_a''(0)]\phi^a+O\left(  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}ight).$$ Because of the choice of $a$, we have that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$. Thus adding the previous two lines we conclude that $v$ is a solution of  egin{equation*}\left\{ egin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\ & rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u} +W''(0) v=M(x) &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega, \end{split}ight.\end{equation*} for some function $M$ satisfying $$\abs{M(x)}=O\left(  rac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}ight) .$$ Therefore, \eqref{eq::6} follows from Corollary ef{cor-comparison} (comparison principle for smooth solutions) and the fact that $W''(0)>0$. The proof of Theorem ef{th::5} is completed due to the fact that a smooth, bounded solution $u$ of \eqref{smooth-solution}, with trace $\phi$, is a viscosity solution in the sense of Definition ef{defi::1} of $$L \phi -W'(\phi)=0\quad \mbox{in }\mathbb R,$$ with $L$ defined through the L'evy-Khintchine formula, as it is noted in Lemma ef{lemma-equivalence}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Take the Cabré-Solà-Morales layer and compare it with the explicit Peierls-Nabarro layer $u^a$, $a=1/\alpha$; Corollary 5.13 gives the sharp $1/x$ asymptotics.

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 6.1
nodes.statement: As we have noted in Theorem \ref{th::3}, the trace of functions in $H$ is a well defined function in $H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. In particular, the trace mapping $T:H\to L^2(\mathbb R)$ is continuous by Sobolev embedding (Theorem \ref{Sobolev}). Then, if we have a sequence $\{u_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\to u_0$ in $H$ with $u_k\in H_0$, then $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'(u_k-u_0)}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{u_k-u_0}^2\right)^{1/2}\to 0\quad\mbox{when } k\to \infty,$$ using the bounds for $\phi'$ given in \eqref{asymptotics}. We conclude that $u_0\in H_0$, and the lemma is shown.
nodes.statement_short: Continuity of the trace into $L^2$ and Cauchy-Schwarz against $\phi'\in L^2$.

Now, given $u,v\in H$, we define the bilinear functional  egin{equation} B(u,v):=\int_\Omega

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2 (existence and regularity of the corrector)
nodes.statement:
Here we seek a solution for  egin{equation} L\psi -W''(\phi)\psi= g \end{equation} where $$g:=\phi'+\eta(W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \eta= rac{\int (\phi')^2}{W''(0)}.$$ It is easy to check that $$g\in H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R),\quad\int_{\partial\Omega} g\phi'=0.$$ We define also the continuous linear functional on $H$ given by $$Ev:=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gTv.$$ The previous Corollary ef{cor-coercivity} asserts that the bilinear functional $B$ from \eqref{bilinear-functional} is coercive on the space $H_0$. Then, Lax-Milgram theorem can be applied to obtain a unique weak solution $u_0\in H$ such that $B(u_0,v)=Ev$ for all $v\in H$. Moreover, the solution depends continuously on the initial datum: $$
orm{u_0}_H\leq C 
orm{g}_{H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)}.$$ We set $\psi:=Tu_0\in H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$.\ The following theorem summarizes its regularity and properties:  egin{theo} The solution $\psi\in H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$ of (ef{eq:20}) has regularity $\mathcal C^{1, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)\cap L^\infty (\hbox{ f R})$, satisfies $\psi(\pm\infty)=0$ and $
orm{\psi'}_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb R)}<\infty$. \end{theo}  egin{proof} Note that $u_0\in H$ so, in particular, $\psi\in H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$ (and is also in all $L^p(\mathbb R)$ for $p>1$).\ \emph{Claim 1:} $\psi$ is bounded; as a consequence, also $u_0$. This follows from Corollary ef{cor-Moser}, after estimating the norm of $g$. We use the asymptotic behavior and boundedness of $\phi,\phi'$ from Theorem ef{th::5}, and the H"{o}lder regularity of $W''$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R} \abs{g}^{p}\leq \int_{(-R,R)} c^{p}+\int_{\mathbb R ackslash (-R,R)}  rac{c^{p}}{\abs{x}^{p eta}}\leq c^{p}\left[ 2R+ rac{2}{(p eta-1)R^{p eta-1}}ight].$$ In particular, for $R=1$, and $p> rac{1}{ eta}$ we have, $$
orm{g}_{L^{p}(\mathbb R)}\leq K c.$$ \emph{Claim 2: } $\mathcal C^{1, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ regularity for $\psi$ follows from Proposition ef{prop-regularity}, while the uniform bound for $\psi'$ is a consequence of Corollary ef{cor-regularity}. For the values of $\psi$ at infinity, just note that $\psi$ is a smooth function in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.\end{proof} \qed Finally, a weak solution $\psi\in H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)\cap \mathcal C^{1, eta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)\cap L^\infty (\hbox{ f R})$ of \eqref{eq:20} is actually a viscosity solution of the equation \eqref{eq::7}, thus completing the proof of Theorem ef{th::6}. This is so because of Lemma ef{lemma-equivalence}.
nodes.statement_short: Lax-Milgram on $H_0$ using the coercivity of $B$ gives a weak corrector; Theorem 6.4 gives its regularity and Lemma 5.6 makes it a viscosity solution.

nodes.statement: Note that $u_0\in H$ so, in particular, $\psi\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$ (and is also in all $L^p(\mathbb R)$ for $p>1$).\\ \emph{Claim 1:} $\psi$ is bounded; as a consequence, also $u_0$. This follows from Corollary \ref{cor-Moser}, after estimating the norm of $g$. We use the asymptotic behavior and boundedness of $\phi,\phi'$ from Theorem \ref{th::5}, and the H\"{o}lder regularity of $W''$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R} \abs{g}^{p}\leq \int_{(-R,R)} c^{p}+\int_{\mathbb R\backslash (-R,R)} \frac{c^{p}}{\abs{x}^{p\beta}}\leq c^{p}\left[ 2R+\frac{2}{(p\beta-1)R^{p\beta-1}}\right].$$ In particular, for $R=1$, and $p>\frac{1}{\beta}$ we have, $$\norm{g}_{L^{p}(\mathbb R)}\leq K c.$$ \emph{Claim 2: } $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ regularity for $\psi$ follows from Proposition \ref{prop-regularity}, while the uniform bound for $\psi'$ is a consequence of Corollary \ref{cor-regularity}. For the values of $\psi$ at infinity, just note that $\psi$ is a smooth function in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.

nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1: $|x-\overline{x}_i(0)|\ge \varepsilon A$ for each $i=1,...,N$}\\ Using the fact that $\phi$ is increasing, we deduce that $\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_i(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_i^0}{\varepsilon}\right)}$ and then using (\ref{eq::10}), we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$

nodes.name: Case 2: near a layer
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2: $|x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)| < \varepsilon A$ for some index $i_0\in \left\{1,...,N\right\}$}\\ Then $$\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)\ge \phi(-A)>0$$ while $$\begin{array}{ll} \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right)} & = \displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)-\delta}{\varepsilon}\right)}\\ \\ & \displaystyle{\le \phi\left(A-\frac{\delta}{\varepsilon}\right) = O\left(\frac{\varepsilon}{\delta}\right) \quad \mbox{as}\quad \varepsilon \to 0.} \end{array}$$ Therefore for $\varepsilon$ small enough, we have $$\displaystyle{\phi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right) \ge \phi\left(\frac{x-{x}_{i_0}^0}{\varepsilon}\right) +\sum_{i=1}^N \varepsilon \overline{c}_i(0) \psi\left(\frac{x-\overline{x}_{i}(0)}{\varepsilon}\right)}.$$ Using again the monotonicity of $\phi$, we conclude in case 2 that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x)\ge v_0^\varepsilon(x).$$

nodes.name: Case 1: near layer $i_0$
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 1: $|x-\overline{x}_{i_0}(t)|\le \varepsilon^{\frac13}$ for some index $i_0\in \left\{1,...,N\right\}$}\\ Hence for $\varepsilon$ small enough, we also have $$|x-\overline{x}_{i}(t)|\ge \varepsilon^{\frac13} \quad \mbox{for}\quad i \in \left\{1,...,N\right\}\backslash \left\{i_0\right\}.$$ Recall also that by (\ref{eq::6}), we have $$\left|\phi(y)-H(y)+\frac{1}{\alpha \pi y}\right| \quad \le \quad \frac{C}{y^2} \quad \mbox{for all}\quad |y|\ge 1.$$ We deduce that $$\left| \sum_{i\not= i_0} \left\{\frac{\tilde{\phi}_i}{\varepsilon} + \frac{1}{\alpha \pi (x-\overline{x}_i)}\right\} \right| \le (N-1) C \varepsilon^{\frac13} = O(\varepsilon^{\frac13}).$$ Therefore using (\ref{eq::12}) $$\begin{array}{lcl} I^\varepsilon & \ge & \displaystyle{e^\varepsilon_{i_0} + O(\varepsilon^{\frac13}) + \alpha \tilde{\sigma}-\sigma}\\ \\ & & \displaystyle{+ 0(\tilde{\phi}_{i_0})\left\{ \frac{1}{\alpha}(\delta + \sigma(t,x)) -\sum_{i\not=i_0} \frac{1}{\alpha\pi (\overline{x}_{i_0}-\overline{x}_i)} + \frac{1}{\alpha \gamma} \overline{c}_{i_0}\right\}}\\ \\ & \ge & \displaystyle{e^\varepsilon_{i_0} + O(\varepsilon^{\frac13}) + \delta + 0(\tilde{\phi}_{i_0})\left\{ \sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,\overline{x}_{i_0})\right\}}\\ \\ & \ge & \delta + O(\varepsilon^{\frac13}) + e^\varepsilon_{i_0}\\ \\ & \ge & \delta/2 \quad \mbox{for}\quad \varepsilon \quad \mbox{small enough} \end{array}$$ where in the first inequality we have used the fact that $\alpha \gamma \eta =1$. To get the last line, we have used the fact that $e^\varepsilon_{i_0} \to 0$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Use the $1/x$ asymptotics (3.7) to reproduce the ODE interaction and get $I^\varepsilon\ge\delta/2$
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Case 2: far from all layers
nodes.statement: {\bf Case 2: $|x-\overline{x}_{i}(t)|\ge \varepsilon^{\frac13}$ for each $i=1,...,N$}\\ Using in particular that $$\tilde{\phi}_i = O(\varepsilon^{\frac23})$$ we conclude again from (\ref{eq::12}) that $$I^\varepsilon \ge \delta/2 \quad \mbox{for}\quad \varepsilon \quad \mbox{small enough}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Away from layers $\tilde\phi_i=O(\varepsilon^{2/3})$, so again $I^\varepsilon\ge\delta/2$
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Finally case 1 and 2 prove that for $\varepsilon$ small enough we have $$I^\varepsilon \ge \delta/2 \quad \mbox{for every}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ which ends the proof of the Proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Both cases give the supersolution inequality
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Step 1: existence and uniqueness
nodes.statement: {\bf Step 1: existence and uniqueness of the solution}\\ First remark that for $\varepsilon$ small enough the initial condition satisfies $$-1\le v^\varepsilon_0 \le N+1$$ and the functions $$\underline{u}(t,x)=-1-K^\varepsilon t \quad \mbox{and}\quad \overline{u}(t,x)=N+1+K^\varepsilon t$$ with $$K^\varepsilon=\varepsilon^{-1}|\sigma|_{L^\infty([0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R})} +\varepsilon^{-2} |W'|_{L^\infty(\hbox{\bf R})}$$ are respectively sub and supersolutions of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. From the Perron's method, it follows the existence of a solution $v^\varepsilon$ of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$ which is moreover unique thanks to the comparison principle (Proposition \ref{pro:4}).
nodes.statement_short: Linear-in-time barriers, Perron's method and the comparison principle
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Step 2: passing to the limit
nodes.statement: {\bf Step 2: sub and supersolutions as $\varepsilon \to 0$}\\ Now, given any fixed $T>0$, and thanks to Propositions \ref{pro::2} and \ref{pro::3}, we can find some $\delta>0$ small enough such that $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ is a supersolution of (\ref{eq::1}) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$.\\ Similarly we can build a subsolution $\underline{v}^\varepsilon$ (defined simply as $\overline{v}^\varepsilon$ but with $\delta <0$). At the initial time we have $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(0,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(0,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}$$ and then from the comparison principle, we get that $$\overline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge v^\varepsilon(t,x) \ge \underline{v}^\varepsilon(t,x) \quad \mbox{for all}\quad t\in [0,T),\quad x\in\hbox{\bf R}.$$ Now for fixed $T>0$, we get the result (namely (\ref{eq::c+}) and (\ref{eq::c-})) on $[0,T)\times \hbox{\bf R}$, passing to the limit as $\varepsilon\to 0$. Finally, because $T>0$ was arbitrary, we recover the result for all time on $[0,+\infty)\times \hbox{\bf R}$. This ends the proof of the Theorem.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Trap $v^\varepsilon$ between $\underline v^\varepsilon$ and $\overline v^\varepsilon$ and let $\varepsilon\to0$
nodes.section: 4 The convergence result: proof of Theorem 1.1

nodes.name: Recall the trace inequality
nodes.statement: For $u$ smooth and with compact support, the classical embedding trace inequality reads \begin{equation} \norm{Tu}^2_{\dot{H}^{\frac{1}{2}}(\hbox{\bf R})}:=\int_{\mathbb R\times \mathbb R}dxdx' \ \frac{|Tu(x')-Tu(x)|^2}{|x'-x|^2}\leq 2\pi \int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2\,dxdy.\end{equation} A proof of the previous inequality can be found in corollary 6.3 in \cite{Alberti-Bouchitte-Seppecher:Phase-transition}.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the classical trace inequality for smooth $u$
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Harmonic extension of functions in $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$

nodes.name: Combine with norm identities
nodes.statement: Then \eqref{trace-mapping} follows by putting together the previous line with \eqref{H12-norm} and \eqref{eq::200}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine with (5.2) and (5.3)
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Harmonic extension of functions in $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$

nodes.name: Density
nodes.statement: For a general $u$ the result follows by density, while the equality case is dealt with in Theorem \ref{th::4} below.
nodes.statement_short: Extend by density; equality case via Theorem 5.4
nodes.section: 5.2.2 Harmonic extension of functions in $H^{\frac12}(\hbox{\bf R})$

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: We recall estimate \eqref{eq::5}. It shows that $\phi'\in L^2(\mathbb R)$. To complete the proof of the first claim we need to check that $\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla \bar u}^2<\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi'\in L^2$; it remains to bound the Dirichlet energy of $\bar u$

nodes.name: Step 1: energy near the boundary
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1: $\int_{\left\{0<y<R\right\}}|\nabla \bar u|^2 < +\infty$.}\\ We proceed as in the proof of Lemma 2.3 in \cite{Cabre-SolaMorales:layer-solutions}. We first set $$v(x,y)=\int_0^y \bar u(x,t)dt.$$ We can see that $v$ is a (smooth) solution of $$\left\{\begin{array}{ll} \Delta v=W''(\phi(x))\phi'(x) &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega, \\ v(x,0)=0 & \quad\mbox{on }\partial\Omega. \end{array}\right.$$ We know (\ref{gradient-bound}) which implies that $v\in L^2\left(\hbox{\bf R}\times [0,R]\right)$. Because the right hand side of the equation is bounded in $L^2(\mathbb R\times [0,R])$, and here we are using again the precise decay of $\phi'$, then we get also that $v\in W^{2,2}_{loc}$ using the boundary gradient estimates for harmonic functions in \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, Lemma 9.12. As a consequence, $\bar u\in W^{1,2}(\hbox{\bf R}\times [0,R])$.
nodes.statement_short: Auxiliary Dirichlet problem and boundary $W^{2,2}$ estimates

nodes.name: Step 2: energy far from the boundary
nodes.statement:
\emph{Step 2: $\int_{\left\{y>Right\}}|
abla  ar u|^2 < +\infty$.}\ Far away from the boundary of $\Omega$, we can use standard interior gradient estimates (Lemma ef{local-grad-estimates}) for the harmonic function $ ar u$, say, at a ball $B_{1}(x,y)\subset \Omega$ so that $$\abs{
abla  ar u(x,y)}\leq C 
orm{ ar u}_{L^\infty (B_{1}(x,y))}\le  rac{C'}{1+(|(x,y)|-1)^2}$$ where we have used (ef{gradient-bound}) in the last inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Interior gradient estimates with the decay (5.16)

nodes.name: Step 3: conclusion of part 1
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 3: Conclusion.}\\ From Steps 1 and 2, we get that $\bar u\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: $\bar u\in H$

nodes.name: Step 4: weak equation
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 4: Proof of (\ref{eq::907}).}\\ From (\ref{Cabre-SolaMorales-layer}) with $f=-W'$, we get for any $w\in C^\infty_c(\overline{\Omega})$: $$0=\int_{\Omega}\nabla u\cdot\nabla w +\int_{\partial \Omega} wW'(u)$$ Setting $w=v_x$ with $v\in C^\infty_c(\overline{\Omega})$, we get by integration by parts $$B(\bar u,v)=0$$ Finally, we conclude by density of $C^\infty_c(\overline{\Omega})$ in $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate the layer equation in $x$ (test with $v_x$) and conclude by density

nodes.name: Choose comparison function
nodes.statement: Fix $a:=2/\tau$, and consider the model layer solution $u^a$ given in \eqref{model-layer}, with trace $\phi^a$. Because of hypothesis on $M$ and the decay of $(\phi^a)_x$ from \eqref{derivative-bound}, we can find a positive constant $K$ such that $\abs{M(x)}\leq K \phi^{a}_x(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Take the model layer with $a=2/\tau$ and bound $|M|$ by $K\phi^a_x$
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions

nodes.name: Robin inequality
nodes.statement:
Next, compute $$ rac{\partial v}{\partial 
u}+d(x) v=M(x)\leq K u^{a}_x\leq K\left[ rac{2}{	au} rac{\partial u_x^{a}}{\partial
u}+2u_x^{a}ight]\leq  rac{2K}{	au} \left[ rac{\partial u_x^{a}}{\partial
u}+d(x) u_x^{a}ight]\quad\mbox{along }\partial\Omega,$$ where we have used \eqref{computation-layer} in the second inequality.
nodes.statement_short: Show $Ku^a_x$ is a supersolution of the Robin problem
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions

nodes.name: Apply strong comparison
nodes.statement: Now we apply Lemma \ref{lema-comparison} to the difference $\left[\frac{2K}{\tau}u_x^{a}-v\right]$ to get $v\le \frac{2K}{\tau}u_x^{a}$ in $\bar\Omega$. The same argument, applied to $-v$ gives that $\abs{v}\le \frac{2K}{\tau}u_x^{a}$.
nodes.statement_short: Comparison principle gives $|v|\le\frac{2K}{\tau}u^a_x$
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Taking into account the estimate \eqref{derivative-bound}, we achieve the conclusion of the corollary.
nodes.statement_short: Decay of $u^a_x$ gives the bound
nodes.section: 5.5 Comparison principles for smooth enough solutions

nodes.name: Reference to classical proof
nodes.statement: This is a small variation of the classical proof for the Laplacian, that can be found in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, Theorem 8.1. Note that $(Tu)^-= T(u^-)$ a.e. in $\mathbb R$.
nodes.statement_short: Follows Gilbarg-Trudinger Thm 8.1

nodes.name: Supports of negative parts
nodes.statement: Set $$\Omega^-:=supp (u^-)\quad\mbox{and}\quad\Theta:=supp((Tu)^-)\subset \mathbb R.$$ We know that $\Omega^-$ is contained in $\mathbb R^2_+\backslash B_R^+$ and $\Theta\subset \mathbb R\backslash(-R,R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Negative parts are supported outside $B_R^+$

nodes.name: Test with $u^-$
nodes.statement: Use $u^-\in H$ as an admissible test function in \eqref{weak-super-solution}; then $$0\leq -\int_{\Omega^-} \abs{\nabla u}^2-\int_{\Theta}d(x)u^2.$$ The proof is easily completed.
nodes.statement_short: Testing with $u^-$ forces $u^-=0$

nodes.name: Moser iteration reference
nodes.statement: This is the classical proof by Moser for the Laplacian case. We follow closely the arguments from Theorems 8.15 and 8.18 in Gilbarg-Trudinger \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}, so we will not give every single detail here.
nodes.statement_short: Follows Gilbarg-Trudinger Thms 8.15, 8.18

nodes.name: Test function $(u^+)^\sigma$
nodes.statement: Assume that $w$ is a subsolution, and set $u:=P*_x w$. Given $\sigma\ge 1$, we insert into \eqref{weak-sub-solution}, the test function $$v=(u^+)^\sigma.$$ Note that $Tv=(Tu)^\sigma$ a.e.. Here we point out that this $v$ might not belong to $H$; in order to make the argument rigorous, a truncated version must be used instead in the definition of $v$, say replacing $u^+$ by \begin{equation} \min\{u^+,n\},\quad \mbox{for}\quad n\in \mathbb N. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Insert truncated powers of $u^+$ as test functions

nodes.name: Energy inequality
nodes.statement_short: Derive $\int|\nabla u_1|^2\le C_1(\gamma)\int w_1^2$

nodes.name: Trace and Sobolev
nodes.statement: For the left hand side, we proceed as follows. We use the trace inequality \eqref{trace-inequality} to estimate $$\frac{1}{2\pi}\norm{w_1}^2_{\dot H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)} \le \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2.$$ But, on the other hand, by Theorem \ref{Sobolev}, for every $p>1$, there exists a constant $C_p>0$ such that $$\begin{array}{ll} ||w_1||^2_{L^{2p}}&\le C_p\left(||w_1||^2_{L^2}+||w_1||^2_{\dot{H}^{\frac12}}\right)\\ \\ &\le C_2(\gamma) ||w_1||^2_{L^2} \quad \mbox{with}\quad C_2(\gamma)=C_p(1+2\pi C_1(\gamma)), \end{array}$$ where we have used \eqref{moser-1} in the last line.
nodes.statement_short: Trace inequality plus Sobolev embedding give an $L^{2p}$ bound

nodes.name: Reverse Hölder step
nodes.statement: If we denote $$\Psi (q):=\left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{w^+}^{q}\right)^{\frac{1}{q}},$$ then we have shown that $$\Psi(2p\gamma)\leq \left[C_2(\gamma)\right]^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\Psi(2\gamma).$$
nodes.statement_short: One step of the iteration: $\Psi(2p\gamma)\le C\Psi(2\gamma)$

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: Fixed $p>1$ and choose $\gamma_m=p^m$ for $m\in\hbox{\bf N}$; by iteration we know \begin{equation} \Psi(2\gamma_m)\leq C_m\Psi(2),\quad \forall m\in\mathbb N\backslash\left\{0\right\},\quad C_m:=\prod_{j=0}^{m-1} \left[C_2(\gamma_j)\right]^\frac{1}{2\gamma_j}.\end{equation} It is then easy to check that $C_m\le C_\infty$ uniformly bounded in $m\in\mathbb N$ (which is also shown, for instance, in page 190 of \cite{Gilbarg-Trudinger}).
nodes.statement_short: Iterate with $\gamma_m=p^m$; constants stay bounded

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Remark that $$\sup_{(-R,R)} \abs{w^+}=\lim_{q\to\infty} \left(\frac{1}{2R} \int_{(-R,R)} \abs{w^+}^q\right)^{\frac{1}{q}}.$$ Letting $m$ to infinity in \eqref{iteration-step}, we have $$\sup_{(-R,R)} \abs{w^+}\leq C_\infty \norm{w^+}_{L^{2}(\mathbb R)},$$ for every $R>0$. We get the first part of the conclusion, taking $R\to +\infty$ and then $n\to +\infty$ in (\ref{eq::902}).
nodes.statement_short: Let $m\to\infty$, $R\to\infty$, $n\to\infty$

nodes.name: Remaining parts
nodes.statement: The second part is analogous, using $u^-$ instead. The final assertion is an immediate consequence of Theorem \ref{thm-Stein}.
nodes.statement_short: Supersolution case analogous; boundedness of $u$ by Theorem 5.7

nodes.name: Adapt Moser iteration
nodes.statement: We use Proposition \ref{prop-moser-iteration} with some modifications in order to account for the extra right hand side term involving $g$. By hypothesis, $w$ is a weak solution satisfying for all $v\in H$, $$B(u,v)=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gv, \quad\mbox{for }u=P*_x w.$$
nodes.statement_short: Modify the Moser argument to include the source $g$

nodes.name: Hölder estimate
nodes.statement: Similarly as before (using if necessary a truncated version), we use the test function $v=\abs{u}^{\sigma-1} u$, $u_1=|u|^{\gamma-1}u$ and $w_1 = Tu_1$. We use H\"older inequality with exponents $2\gamma$, $\frac{2\gamma}{2\gamma-1}$, which gives $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} gv}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{g}^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\right)^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}},$$ we get \begin{equation*}\begin{split} \int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 &\le C_1(\gamma) \int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2} +\tilde{C}_1(\gamma)\left(\int_{\partial\Omega} w_1^{2}\right)^{\frac{2\gamma-1}{2\gamma}}\quad \mbox{with}\quad \tilde{C}_1(\gamma)= \frac{\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}\cdot \left(\int_{\partial \Omega} |g|^{2\gamma}\right)^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}. \end{split}\end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Hölder inequality bounds the source term

nodes.name: Uniform constant
nodes.statement: Assuming (\ref{eq::904}) with $2\gamma\ge p_0$, we get $$\int_{\Omega} \abs{\nabla u_1}^2 \le \bar{C}_1(\gamma) \max\left\{1,\int_{\partial \Omega} w_1^2\right\} \quad \mbox{with}\quad \bar{C}_1(\gamma) = C_1(\gamma) + \frac{c\gamma^2}{2\gamma-1}$$
nodes.statement_short: Uniform $L^p$ bound on $g$ gives an energy bound

nodes.name: Iterate
nodes.statement: The rest of the argument follows similarly, with $\bar{C}_2(\gamma)=\max\left\{1,C_p(1+2\pi \bar{C}_1(\gamma))\right\}$, $\bar\Psi(q)=\max \left\{1,\left(\int_{\partial\Omega}|w|^q\right)^{\frac1q}\right\}$, and $\bar \Psi(2p\gamma)\le (\bar C_2(\gamma))^{\frac{1}{2\gamma}}\bar \Psi(2\gamma)$, starting the iteration at $2\gamma=p_0$.\qed
nodes.statement_short: Iterate as before starting at $2\gamma=p_0$

nodes.name: Layer from Cabré-Solà-Morales
nodes.statement: Let $W$ be a potential satisfying hypothesis \emph{Ai)}. Theorem \ref{thm-layer-solutions} shows existence, regularity, uniqueness and asymptotic behavior of a layer solution $0<u_W<1$ satisfying $u_W(0,0)=1/2$, $u\in\mathcal C^{2,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline{\Omega})$, for the problem \begin{equation} \left\{\begin{split} \Delta u &= 0 &\quad \mbox{in } \Omega,\\ \frac{\partial u}{\partial \nu} &= -W'(u) &\quad \mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.\end{equation} We denote its trace value by $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$. The aim of the next paragraphs is to show the more precise estimate \eqref{eq::6} for the asymptotic behavior near infinity.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 5.10 gives the layer $u_W$ with trace $\phi$

nodes.name: Compare with the model layer
nodes.statement: Set $a=1/\alpha$, where $\alpha=W''(0)$ as defined in (\ref{eq::900}), and choose the model layer solution $u^a$ as given in \eqref{model-layer}. We know explicitly because of \eqref{asymptotic-layer} that $\phi^a:=u^a(\cdot,0)$ has the right asymptotic behavior \eqref{eq::6}. We would like to compare $u_W$ to $u^a$, in order to obtain the analogous estimate for $u_W$. Therefore, we set $v:=u_W-u^a$. Then $v$ satisfies \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v= \;0 \quad &\mbox{in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu}= -W'(\phi)+V'_a(\phi^a)\quad &\mbox{on } \partial\Omega. \end{split}\right. \end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Set $v=u_W-u^a$ with $a=1/\alpha$

nodes.name: Robin equation for $v$
nodes.statement: Now we estimate $$-W'(\phi)+W'(\phi^a)=-W''(0)[\phi-\phi^a]+O\left( \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\right),$$ thanks to the growth estimate \eqref{growth-not-sharp}. And also, $$-W'(\phi^a)+V'_a(\phi^a)=[-W''(0)+V_a''(0)]\phi^a+O\left( \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\right).$$ Because of the choice of $a$, we have that $W''(0)=V_a''(0)$. Thus adding the previous two lines we conclude that $v$ is a solution of \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} +W''(0) v=M(x) &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega, \end{split}\right.\end{equation*} for some function $M$ satisfying $$\abs{M(x)}=O\left( \frac{1}{1+\abs{x}^2}\right) .$$
nodes.statement_short: Linearize to get $\partial_\nu v+W''(0)v=M$ with $M=O((1+x^2)^{-1})$

nodes.name: Apply Corollary 5.13
nodes.statement: Therefore, \eqref{eq::6} follows from Corollary \ref{cor-comparison} (comparison principle for smooth solutions) and the fact that $W''(0)>0$.
nodes.statement_short: Decay of $v$ gives (3.7)

nodes.name: Viscosity solution
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem \ref{th::5} is completed due to the fact that a smooth, bounded solution $u$ of \eqref{smooth-solution}, with trace $\phi$, is a viscosity solution in the sense of Definition \ref{defi::1} of $$L \phi -W'(\phi)=0\quad \mbox{in }\mathbb R,$$ with $L$ defined through the L\'evy-Khintchine formula, as it is noted in Lemma \ref{lemma-equivalence}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Smooth solution is a viscosity solution by Lemma 5.6

nodes.name: Continuity of the trace
nodes.statement: As we have noted in Theorem \ref{th::3}, the trace of functions in $H$ is a well defined function in $H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. In particular, the trace mapping $T:H\to L^2(\mathbb R)$ is continuous by Sobolev embedding (Theorem \ref{Sobolev}).
nodes.statement_short: The trace $H\to L^2$ is continuous

nodes.name: Pass to the limit
nodes.statement: Then, if we have a sequence $\{u_k\}_{k=1}^\infty\to u_0$ in $H$ with $u_k\in H_0$, then $$\abs{\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'(u_k-u_0)}\leq \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'^2\right)^{1/2} \left(\int_{\partial\Omega} \abs{u_k-u_0}^2\right)^{1/2}\to 0\quad\mbox{when } k\to \infty,$$ using the bounds for $\phi'$ given in \eqref{asymptotics}.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz with $\phi'\in L^2$

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: We conclude that $u_0\in H_0$, and the lemma is shown.
nodes.statement_short: Limit lies in $H_0$

nodes.name: Interpolation
nodes.statement: It easily follows from Lemma \ref{lem:1}. Indeed, \begin{equation*} \begin{split} B(u,u) & =\int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega}W''(\phi)u^2\geq (1-\mu) C_0 \int_{\partial\Omega} u^2+\mu Q(u)\\ & \geq \mu\int_\Omega \abs{\nabla u}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} u^2\left[(1-\mu)C_0+\mu W''(\phi)\right].\\ \end{split}\end{equation*}
nodes.statement_short: Split $B(u,u)$ using Lemma 6.2

nodes.name: Choose $\mu$
nodes.statement: Because $W''$ is bounded, there exists $\mu>0$ small enough such that $(1-\mu)C_0+\mu W''(\phi)>\tfrac{C_0}{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $\mu$ small

nodes.name: Conclusion
nodes.statement: Therefore, \begin{equation} B(u,u)\geq\min\left\{\mu,\tfrac{C_0}{2}\right\} \norm{u}_H^2, \end{equation} as claimed.
nodes.statement_short: Coercivity (6.5)

nodes.name: Outline
nodes.statement: It is divided into several steps:
nodes.statement_short: Outline of the steps

nodes.name: Step 1: stability
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 1: Stability.} Because of the construction of $u_W$ and $\phi$, we know from Theorem \ref{thm-layer-solutions} that $Q(u)\geq 0$ for all $u\in \mathcal C_c^\infty(\bar\Omega)$ (i.e. layer solutions are stable). Thus the functional $Q$ is bounded from below also in $H$.
nodes.statement_short: Stability of layer solutions gives $Q\ge0$

nodes.name: Step 2: existence of a minimizer
nodes.statement_short: Existence of a constrained minimizer of $Q$ on $H_0$

nodes.name: Step 2.1: minimizing sequence
nodes.statement_short: Split $Q=Q_1+Q_2$, take a bounded minimizing sequence, extract weak and locally strong limits

nodes.name: Step 2.2: identify the limit
nodes.statement:
\emph{Step 2.2: Concluding.}\ \emph{Case A: $u_0\equiv 0$}\ Remark first that $$Q_1(u_k)\ge 	au \int_{\partial \Omega} u_k^2 = 	au >0.$$ On the other hand, we have $Q_2(u_k)	o Q_2(u_0)=0$. Therefore we get $$\liminf_{k	o\infty} Q(u_k) = \liminf_{k	o\infty} \left\{Q_1(u_k)+ Q_2(u_k)ight\} \ge 	au >0,$$ which is in contradiction with (ef{eq::910}). Therefore only the next case occurs.\ \emph{Case B: $u_0
ot\equiv 0$}\ Then we have $0\le Q_1(u_0)=0$ and we will show that $Tu_k	o T u_0$ in $H^{ rac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$. nodes.name: Step 3: Euler-Lagrange equation
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 3: Euler-Lagrange equation.} Once the minimizer $u_0$ is found, the theory of Lagrange multipliers for minimization problems (see, for instance, \cite{Evans}, chapter 8.4) gives that $u_0\in H$ must be a weak solution of \begin{equation} B(u_0,v)=\lambda \int_{\partial\Omega} u_0v+\mu \int_{\partial\Omega} \phi'v \quad \mbox{ for every } v\in H,\end{equation} where $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$. The value of the multipliers can be found by choosing the right test function $v$. Thus if we test the equality \eqref{Lagrange} with $v=P*_x\phi'$, we obtain $\mu=0$ (see Lemma \ref{properties}), while testing against $v=u_0$ gives that \begin{equation} \lambda=Q(u_0)=\int_{\Omega}\abs{\nabla u_0}^2+\int_{\partial\Omega} W''(\phi)u_0^2 \quad (\geq 0).\end{equation}

nodes.name: Step 5: $\lambda\neq0$
nodes.statement: \emph{Step 5: Positivity.} In the following we show that if $\lambda=0$, then $w_0=Tu_0$ must necessarily be a multiple of $\phi'$, which is a contradiction with the fact that $u_0\in H_0$ and $\int_{\partial \Omega} u_0^2=1$. Thus we take $\lambda=0$ in \eqref{Lagrange}. Then we have a solution $u_0$ satisfying $B(u_0,v)=0$ for all $v\in H$. We remind the reader that have defined $u_W$ to be the layer solution for our potential $W$, with trace $\phi:=u_W(\cdot,0)$, and $\bar u:=\partial_x u_W$, which is also uniformly bounded and has trace $\bar u(\cdot, 0)=\phi'$. Because of the hypothesis on the potential $W$ and the asymptotic behavior of the layer solution $\phi$, there exists some $\tau>0$ such that $W''(\phi)\geq \tau$ on $\mathbb R\backslash[-R,R]$ for some $R>0$. We have shown, in particular, that $u_0$ is uniformly bounded in $\overline{\Omega}$. Since $\bar u$ is positive from \eqref{derivative-positive}, then there exists $\kappa\geq 0$ such that $\abs{u_0}<\kappa \bar u$ in $B^+_R$. We set $v:=\kappa \bar u-u_0$, and note that $v$ satisfies the conditions of Proposition \ref{prop-weak-comparison}. Thus we can conclude that $v\geq 0$ in $\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ so that $u_0\leq\kappa\bar u$. An analogous argument gives that $-u_0<\kappa\bar u$. We have proved that $\abs{u_0}<\kappa\bar u$ on $\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ and, in particular, $\abs{w(x)}<\kappa\phi'(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$.\\ The next step is to decrease $\kappa$ up to the first point where $\kappa\bar u$ touches $\abs{u_0}$: assume, without loss of generality, that for some $\kappa^*\geq 0$ there exists $(x_0,y_0)\in\overline{\mathbb R^2_+}$ such that \begin{equation} \kappa^* \bar u=u_0 \quad \mbox{at }(x_0,y_0)\quad \mbox{and}\quad \kappa^*\bar u \ge u_0 \quad \mbox{on}\quad \overline{\Omega}.\end{equation} We set $d_1:=\max\{W''(\phi),\tau\}$, and $d_2:=d_1-W''(\phi)$. We note that both are non-negative functions on $\mathbb R$ and $d_1(x)\geq \tau$ for all $x\in\mathbb R$. Let $v:=\kappa^*\bar u-u_0\ge 0$, that is a weak supersolution of \begin{equation*}\left\{\begin{split} &\Delta v = 0 \quad &\mbox{ in } \Omega,\\ &\frac{\partial v}{\partial \nu} +d_1 v=d_2 v \geq 0\quad &\mbox{ on }\partial\Omega. \end{split}\right.\end{equation*} We are in the hypothesis of Lemma \ref{lema-comparison}, that can be applied because the functions have enough regularity (in particular $v\in\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\overline\Omega)$). However, because of \eqref{functions-touch} we necessarily must have $v\equiv 0$. We have shown that $u_0\equiv\kappa^*\bar u$, which at the boundary translates as $w\equiv\kappa^*\phi'$.
nodes.statement_short: If $\lambda=0$, a touching argument with $\kappa\bar u$ forces $u_0$ to be a multiple of $\phi'$

nodes.statement: \emph{Step 6: Conclusion.} The multiplier $\lambda$ in \eqref{eq::100} must be non-negative. nodes.statement_short: $C_0=\lambda>0$ and rescaling gives the bound

nodes.name: Corrector equation with source $g$
nodes.statement: Here we seek a solution for \begin{equation} L\psi -W''(\phi)\psi= g \end{equation} where $$g:=\phi'+\eta(W''(\phi)-W''(0)) \quad \mbox{with}\quad \eta=\frac{\int (\phi')^2}{W''(0)}.$$ It is easy to check that $$g\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R),\quad\int_{\partial\Omega} g\phi'=0.$$
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the corrector equation with source $g$ orthogonal to $\phi'$

nodes.name: Lax-Milgram
nodes.statement: We define also the continuous linear functional on $H$ given by $$Ev:=-\int_{\partial\Omega} gTv.$$ The previous Corollary \ref{cor-coercivity} asserts that the bilinear functional $B$ from \eqref{bilinear-functional} is coercive on the space $H_0$. Then, Lax-Milgram theorem can be applied to obtain a unique weak solution $u_0\in H$ such that $B(u_0,v)=Ev$ for all $v\in H$.
nodes.statement_short: Coercivity on $H_0$ and Lax-Milgram give a weak solution

nodes.name: Define $\psi$
nodes.statement: Moreover, the solution depends continuously on the initial datum: $$\norm{u_0}_H\leq C \norm{g}_{H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)}.$$ We set $\psi:=Tu_0\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$.
nodes.statement_short: Continuous dependence; set $\psi=Tu_0$

nodes.name: Regularity theorem
nodes.statement: The following theorem summarizes its regularity and properties: \begin{theo} The solution $\psi\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$ of (\ref{eq:20}) has regularity $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)\cap L^\infty (\hbox{\bf R})$, satisfies $\psi(\pm\infty)=0$ and $\norm{\psi'}_{L^{\infty}(\mathbb R)}<\infty$. \end{theo} \begin{proof} Note that $u_0\in H$ so, in particular, $\psi\in H^{\frac{1}{2}}(\mathbb R)$ (and is also in all $L^p(\mathbb R)$ for $p>1$).\\ \emph{Claim 1:} $\psi$ is bounded; as a consequence, also $u_0$. This follows from Corollary \ref{cor-Moser}, after estimating the norm of $g$. We use the asymptotic behavior and boundedness of $\phi,\phi'$ from Theorem \ref{th::5}, and the H\"{o}lder regularity of $W''$. Then $$\int_{\mathbb R} \abs{g}^{p}\leq \int_{(-R,R)} c^{p}+\int_{\mathbb R\backslash (-R,R)} \frac{c^{p}}{\abs{x}^{p\beta}}\leq c^{p}\left[ 2R+\frac{2}{(p\beta-1)R^{p\beta-1}}\right].$$ In particular, for $R=1$, and $p>\frac{1}{\beta}$ we have, $$\norm{g}_{L^{p}(\mathbb R)}\leq K c.$$ \emph{Claim 2: } $\mathcal C^{1,\beta}_{\mbox{loc}}(\mathbb R)$ regularity for $\psi$ follows from Proposition \ref{prop-regularity}, while the uniform bound for $\psi'$ is a consequence of Corollary \ref{cor-regularity}. For the values of $\psi$ at infinity, just note that $\psi$ is a smooth function in $L^2(\mathbb R)$.\end{proof} \qed

This is so because of Lemma \ref{lemma-equivalence}.
